title: Biology IX — Chapter 2: Molecular Biology
description: Sindh DCAR Biology Curriculum 2024 aligned study course. Covers biomolecules, their structures and functions, nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, and the role of genetic information in protein synthesis. Includes lessons, explained MCQs, CRQs and ERQs with model answers and marking rubrics.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Molecular Biology
chapters.description: How the molecules of life build cells, store information and carry out essential biological processes.

lessons.title: 2.1 Introduction to Molecular Biology and the Chemistry of Life
lessons.content:
## Learning outcomes
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain molecular biology and describe why molecules are essential to living organisms.

## What is molecular biology?
Molecular biology studies life processes at the molecular level. It investigates how DNA stores hereditary information, how RNA helps use that information, how proteins perform many cellular jobs and how molecules interact inside cells.

Living organisms are made from atoms joined into molecules. Water and mineral ions are essential inorganic substances. The major groups of organic biomolecules are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Organic molecules commonly contain carbon bonded with hydrogen and other elements.

## Why molecules matter
- Carbohydrates are important energy sources and may provide structural support.
- Lipids store energy, form cell membranes and help with insulation and signalling.
- Proteins act as enzymes, transporters, antibodies, receptors and structural materials.
- Nucleic acids store, transmit and help express genetic information.

These groups work together. For example, a cell membrane contains lipids and proteins, while the instructions for making many of those proteins are encoded in DNA.

## Building large molecules
Many biological molecules are assembled from smaller subunits. Proteins are polymers of amino acids; nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides; and many carbohydrates are made from sugar units. Lipids are not true polymers made from repeating identical monomers, although many contain fatty acids joined to glycerol.

## Key terms
- **Biomolecule:** a molecule produced by or found in living organisms.
- **Monomer:** a small molecular subunit that can join with others.
- **Polymer:** a large molecule made from many linked subunits.
- **Macromolecule:** a very large molecule, such as a protein or nucleic acid.

## Check your understanding
Why can a cell not rely on only one type of biomolecule? Give one function for each of the four major groups.

lessons.title: 2.2 Carbohydrates and Lipids
lessons.content:
## Learning outcomes
Describe the basic composition and major functions of carbohydrates and lipids, and distinguish between them.

## Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Their building units are simple sugars called monosaccharides. Glucose is an important monosaccharide used in cellular respiration.

Two monosaccharides can join to form a disaccharide. Examples include sucrose and lactose. Many sugar units can join to form a polysaccharide:
- **Starch:** energy-storage carbohydrate in plants.
- **Glycogen:** energy-storage carbohydrate in animals and fungi.
- **Cellulose:** structural carbohydrate in plant cell walls; humans cannot digest it as a source of glucose.

Carbohydrates provide readily available energy and some have structural roles.

## Lipids
Lipids are a diverse group of mostly water-insoluble molecules. A common fat or oil (triglyceride) contains one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids. Lipids contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but usually proportionally less oxygen than carbohydrates.

Functions of lipids include long-term energy storage, thermal insulation, protection of organs and formation of cell membranes. Phospholipids have a water-attracting head and water-repelling tails, allowing them to form a bilayer in watery environments.

## Saturated and unsaturated fatty acids
Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds. The physical state of a fat or oil depends on its fatty-acid composition and temperature; do not assume every plant oil is always liquid under all conditions.

## Comparison
| Feature | Carbohydrates | Lipids |
|---|---|---|
| Common roles | Quick energy; structure | Long-term energy; membranes; insulation |
| Typical subunits | Monosaccharides | Often glycerol and fatty acids in fats |
| Solubility | Many small sugars dissolve in water | Most are poorly soluble in water |

## Application
A runner may use glucose during exercise, while stored fat can provide energy over longer periods. Plant cellulose gives support to stems and leaves.

lessons.title: 2.3 Proteins: Structure and Functions
lessons.content:
## Learning outcomes
Explain that proteins are made of amino acids and describe important functions of proteins in organisms.

## Amino acids and peptide bonds
Proteins are polymers made from amino-acid monomers. Each amino acid has a central carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain (R group). Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptide chains.

The order of amino acids is called the primary structure. The chain folds into a particular three-dimensional shape. This shape is important because it influences the protein's function. Some proteins consist of more than one polypeptide chain.

## Functions of proteins
- **Enzymes:** speed up chemical reactions.
- **Structural proteins:** provide strength, for example collagen in connective tissue and keratin in hair.
- **Transport proteins:** carry substances, for example haemoglobin transports oxygen in blood.
- **Defence proteins:** antibodies help the immune system recognise specific foreign substances.
- **Hormones and receptors:** some proteins act as chemical messengers or receive signals.
- **Movement:** actin and myosin participate in muscle contraction.

## Denaturation
Heat, extreme pH or certain chemicals can disrupt the interactions that maintain a protein's shape. The protein may become denatured and lose its normal function. Denaturation usually changes shape rather than simply breaking every peptide bond.

## Protein-rich foods
Pulses, beans, lentils, eggs, milk, fish, meat, nuts and seeds can provide dietary protein. During digestion, proteins are broken down into amino acids and small peptides that the body absorbs and uses to build its own proteins.

## Check your understanding
Explain why a change in a protein's shape may affect its function. Give two examples of proteins with different roles.

lessons.title: 2.4 Nucleic Acids: DNA and RNA
lessons.content:
## Learning outcomes
Describe the nucleotide as the building unit of nucleic acids and compare DNA with RNA.

## Nucleotides
A nucleotide contains three components: a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogen-containing base. Nucleotides join to form nucleic-acid strands.

## DNA
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) stores hereditary information in most organisms. DNA is usually made of two antiparallel strands twisted into a double helix. Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone and bases facing inward. The bases are adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G.

The sequence of bases carries information. A gene is a region of DNA whose sequence contributes to a functional product, commonly a protein or a functional RNA. DNA is organised with proteins into chromosomes in cells.

## RNA
Ribonucleic acid (RNA) usually consists of a single strand. Its sugar is ribose and it uses uracil (U) instead of thymine. The main bases are A, U, C and G. Several types of RNA help cells use genetic information:
- **Messenger RNA (mRNA):** carries a copy of genetic instructions from DNA to a ribosome.
- **Transfer RNA (tRNA):** brings amino acids to the ribosome and uses its anticodon to pair with an mRNA codon.
- **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA):** forms a major part of ribosomes and helps catalyse peptide-bond formation.

## DNA and RNA compared
| Feature | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Bases | A, T, C, G | A, U, C, G |
| Usual structure | Double-stranded helix | Usually single-stranded |
| Main role | Long-term genetic information storage | Helps express and regulate genetic information |

Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material. The usual comparison above describes cellular DNA and RNA, not every viral genome.

lessons.title: 2.5 From DNA to Protein: Protein Synthesis
lessons.content:
## Learning outcomes
Outline transcription and translation and explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA and ribosomes.

## The central idea
In cells, information in a gene can be used to make a protein. The two main stages are transcription and translation.

**DNA gene → mRNA → polypeptide → functional protein**

## 1. Transcription
In eukaryotic cells, transcription takes place in the nucleus. RNA polymerase uses one DNA strand as a template to build a complementary RNA molecule. RNA contains uracil (U) rather than thymine (T). In eukaryotes, the first RNA transcript is processed before mature mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore. In prokaryotes, transcription occurs in the cytoplasm and translation can begin while the mRNA is still being made.

## 2. Translation
Translation occurs at a ribosome in the cytoplasm or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The ribosome reads the mRNA sequence in groups of three bases called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or a stop signal.

A tRNA molecule carries a particular amino acid. Its anticodon pairs with a complementary mRNA codon. The ribosome helps join amino acids by peptide bonds. Translation usually begins at a start codon (AUG in the standard genetic code) and ends when a stop codon is reached. The polypeptide is then released and folds, and it may be modified or combined with other chains to become a functional protein.

## Simple worked example
If an mRNA segment reads 5′-AUG-GCU-UAA-3′, AUG is a start codon, GCU codes for alanine and UAA is a stop codon. This short message would begin a polypeptide containing methionine followed by alanine, then stop. The example uses the standard genetic code.

## Why protein synthesis matters
Proteins build cell structures, catalyse reactions, transport materials and enable communication. A change in DNA sequence may change an mRNA codon and sometimes an amino acid in a protein. The effect depends on the location and nature of the change; not every DNA change alters a protein or causes disease.

## Review
Explain how the information in DNA can determine the order of amino acids in a protein. Include the terms transcription, mRNA, codon, tRNA, ribosome and translation.

questions.question: Molecular biology mainly investigates life processes at which level?

options.A: Only the level of whole ecosystems
options.B: The molecular level, including DNA, RNA and proteins

questions.explanation: Molecular biology explains biological processes through molecules and their interactions.

questions.question: Which group of biomolecules is made from amino-acid subunits?
questions.explanation: Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptides and proteins.

questions.question: The main storage carbohydrate in plants is:
questions.explanation: Plants store glucose in the form of starch.

questions.question: Which carbohydrate forms much of the plant cell wall?
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide that strengthens plant cell walls.

questions.question: A triglyceride contains:

options.A: Three amino acids and one sugar
options.B: Glycerol joined to three fatty acids

questions.explanation: A common fat molecule is made from glycerol and three fatty acids.

questions.question: Which is a major function of phospholipids?

options.A: Forming the main bilayer of cell membranes

questions.explanation: Phospholipids form bilayers with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.

questions.question: A peptide bond joins:
questions.explanation: Peptide bonds link amino acids in a polypeptide chain.

questions.question: Which protein transports oxygen in human blood?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds and transports oxygen.

questions.question: Why can high temperature cause a protein to lose its function?

options.A: It always changes all amino acids into sugars
options.B: It can disrupt interactions that maintain protein shape
options.D: It removes all peptide bonds instantly

questions.explanation: Heat can disrupt the protein's three-dimensional structure, causing denaturation.

questions.question: A nucleotide is composed of:

options.A: Amino acid, glycerol and fatty acid

questions.explanation: Each nucleotide contains a pentose sugar, phosphate group and nitrogenous base.

questions.question: Which base is present in RNA but not normally in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

questions.question: In DNA, adenine pairs with:
questions.explanation: Complementary DNA base pairing is A–T and C–G.

questions.question: Which type of RNA carries genetic instructions from DNA to a ribosome?
questions.explanation: Messenger RNA carries the copied genetic message to the ribosome.

questions.question: The main role of tRNA during translation is to:

options.B: Carry amino acids and pair its anticodon with mRNA codons

questions.explanation: Transfer RNA brings amino acids to the ribosome and matches anticodons to codons.

questions.question: Transcription is the process of:

options.A: Making RNA using a DNA template

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase uses DNA as a template to synthesise RNA.

questions.question: Translation takes place at:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA codons and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.

questions.question: A codon consists of:
questions.explanation: A codon is a sequence of three nucleotides in mRNA.

questions.question: Which mRNA codon commonly acts as a start codon?
questions.explanation: AUG usually signals the start of translation and codes for methionine.

questions.question: Which statement about a scientific protein is most accurate?

options.A: Its function is unrelated to its shape
options.B: Its amino-acid sequence helps determine its three-dimensional shape

questions.explanation: A protein's amino-acid sequence influences folding and therefore its structure and function.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched?

options.A: DNA—long-term hereditary information; RNA—helps express genetic information

questions.explanation: DNA stores hereditary information while different RNAs participate in gene expression.

writtenQuestions.question: Name the four major groups of organic biomolecules and state one important function of each.
writtenQuestions.modelAnswer: The four groups are carbohydrates (energy supply and some structural roles), lipids (long-term energy storage, membranes and insulation), proteins (enzymes, structure, transport and defence) and nucleic acids (storage and expression of genetic information).
rubric: One accurate function for each group (3 marks)

writtenQuestions.question: Differentiate between DNA and RNA by giving four structural or functional differences.
writtenQuestions.modelAnswer: DNA contains deoxyribose whereas RNA contains ribose. DNA uses thymine whereas RNA uses uracil. DNA is usually double-stranded while RNA is usually single-stranded. DNA mainly stores hereditary information; RNA has roles in carrying, translating and regulating genetic information.

writtenQuestions.question: Explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA in protein synthesis.
writtenQuestions.modelAnswer: mRNA carries the genetic message copied from DNA to the ribosome. tRNA brings specific amino acids and pairs its anticodon with mRNA codons. rRNA forms a major part of the ribosome and helps position molecules and catalyse peptide-bond formation.

writtenQuestions.question: Describe the process of protein synthesis from a gene in DNA to a polypeptide. Include transcription and translation in your answer.
writtenQuestions.modelAnswer: During transcription, RNA polymerase uses a DNA template strand to produce complementary RNA. In eukaryotes the transcript is processed and mature mRNA leaves the nucleus. At a ribosome, translation begins at a start codon. The ribosome reads mRNA codons; tRNAs with complementary anticodons deliver the corresponding amino acids. The ribosome joins amino acids by peptide bonds. Translation ends at a stop codon and the polypeptide is released, folds and may be modified to become functional.
rubric: DNA template and RNA polymerase in transcription (2 marks)
mRNA formation and, where relevant, processing/export (2 marks)
tRNA anticodon and amino-acid delivery (2 marks)
Peptide bonds and chain growth (1 mark)
Stop codon, release and folding (2 marks)

writtenQuestions.question: Compare carbohydrates, lipids and proteins in terms of their building units, examples and functions in living organisms.
writtenQuestions.modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides; examples include glucose, starch, glycogen and cellulose. They supply energy and may provide structure. Many lipids contain glycerol and fatty acids; examples include triglycerides and phospholipids. They store energy, insulate and form cell membranes. Proteins are polymers of amino acids; examples include enzymes, haemoglobin, antibodies and collagen. They catalyse reactions, transport substances, defend the body and provide structure. Their different structures explain their different properties and roles.
rubric: Carbohydrate building units and example (2 marks)
Protein building units and example (2 marks)
Protein functions and clear comparison (2 marks)
